questions.title: Which organism most commonly causes a spinal epidural abscess in an IV drug user?
questions.question: A 25-year-old intravenous drug user presents with fever and back pain. MRI reveals an epidural abscess. Which of the following is the most common causative organism for this type of infection?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Streptococcus pneumoniae is a leading cause of community-acquired bacterial meningitis, not the typical organism in an IV-drug-user epidural abscess.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Neisseria meningitidis causes meningococcal meningitis and septicaemia, not spinal epidural abscess from skin-flora bacteraemia.
explanations.C: Correct. Staphylococcus aureus, seeded from skin flora during non-sterile injection, is the most common cause of spinal epidural abscess in intravenous drug users, presenting with fever, localised back pain and progressive neurological deficit confirmed on MRI. Empirical antibiotic cover for suspected epidural abscess in this population should therefore include anti-staphylococcal activity (e.g. vancomycin) pending cultures.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Mycobacterium tuberculosis can cause a spinal (Pott's) abscess, but this is a chronic, indolent process, not the acute presentation typical of IV-drug-use-associated epidural abscess.

questions.learning_objective: Identify Staphylococcus aureus as the most common cause of spinal epidural abscess in intravenous drug users.

questions.title: A brain abscess following a tooth infection represents which route of CNS entry?
questions.question: A patient presents with a brain abscess following a tooth infection. This represents which primary route of entry for organisms into the central nervous system?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Haematogenous spread is bloodstream seeding from a distant infected site, not direct contiguous spread from an adjacent dental focus.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Direct implantation refers to organisms introduced by trauma or a surgical/iatrogenic breach, not contiguous spread from an adjacent infected structure.
explanations.C: Correct. A dental infection tracking directly into adjacent brain tissue, without an intervening bloodstream step, is local extension — the same route by which sinusitis, otitis media and mastoiditis cause brain abscess. Odontogenic brain abscesses characteristically localise to the frontal or temporal lobe depending on which teeth are involved.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Peripheral nerve spread describes retrograde axonal transport, as with rabies virus, not contiguous spread from a nearby infected structure.

questions.learning_objective: Classify a brain abscess following a dental infection as spread by local extension.

questions.title: Which CSF profile is most consistent with acute bacterial meningitis?
questions.question: A patient presents with acute bacterial meningitis. Which of the following cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) findings is most consistent with this diagnosis?

options.A: Normal glucose, elevated lymphocytes, clear appearance
options.B: Decreased glucose, elevated neutrophils, turbid appearance
options.C: Normal glucose, elevated neutrophils, normal protein
options.D: Decreased glucose, elevated lymphocytes, cobweb formation

explanations.A: Incorrect. Normal glucose with a lymphocytic pleocytosis and clear CSF describes viral (aseptic) meningitis, not bacterial meningitis.
explanations.B: Correct. Decreased glucose (from bacterial and neutrophil consumption), a neutrophil-predominant pleocytosis and turbid/purulent CSF is the classic profile of acute pyogenic bacterial meningitis. A Gram stain and culture of this turbid CSF typically identify the causative organism and guide targeted antibiotic therapy.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Normal glucose with normal protein is inconsistent with acute bacterial meningitis, which characteristically depletes glucose and raises protein.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Decreased glucose with lymphocytic predominance and cobweb clot formation is the classic profile of tuberculous meningitis, not acute pyogenic bacterial meningitis.

questions.learning_objective: State the characteristic CSF profile of acute bacterial meningitis: decreased glucose, neutrophilic pleocytosis, turbid appearance.

questions.title: Diffuse neonatal encephalitis after vaginal delivery to a mother with active genital lesions — which virus?
questions.question: A neonate presents with diffuse encephalitis after a vaginal delivery. The mother has a history of active genital lesions. Which viral agent is the most likely cause?

explanations.A: Incorrect. HSV-1 more typically causes focal temporal-lobe encephalitis in older children and adults, transmitted orally, not the diffuse neonatal disease from an infected birth canal.
explanations.B: Correct. HSV-2, transmitted perinatally through an infected birth canal from a mother with active genital lesions, is the most likely cause of diffuse, often severe neonatal encephalitis. Untreated neonatal HSV encephalitis carries high mortality and severe neurological morbidity, so intravenous aciclovir is started empirically pending confirmatory testing.
explanations.C: Incorrect. HIV can be transmitted perinatally but causes a progressive encephalopathy over months to years, not an acute diffuse encephalitis at birth.
explanations.D: Incorrect. JC virus causes progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy in immunocompromised patients, an entity unrelated to perinatal transmission or neonatal encephalitis.

questions.learning_objective: Identify HSV-2 as the most likely cause of diffuse neonatal encephalitis after vaginal delivery to a mother with active genital herpetic lesions.

questions.title: In a diabetic patient, CNS mucormycosis most often spreads to the brain via which route?
questions.question: A patient with a history of diabetes presents with encephalitis. The most likely route of infection for Mucormycosis in this patient is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Mucormycosis is angioinvasive but its classic rhinocerebral route into the brain is by contiguous spread, not primary bloodstream dissemination from a distant site.
explanations.B: Correct. Rhinocerebral mucormycosis, classically seen in poorly controlled diabetics, begins in the nasal mucosa and sinuses and spreads by direct extension into the orbit and brain. Prompt surgical debridement alongside amphotericin B is required because mucormycosis progresses rapidly and is often fatal if treatment is delayed.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Iatrogenic direct implantation refers to organisms introduced by a surgical or procedural breach, not spread from an adjacent sinus infection.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Travel through peripheral nerves is the route used by rabies virus, not the fungal invasion pattern of mucormycosis.

questions.learning_objective: State that CNS mucormycosis in a diabetic patient most often reaches the brain by direct extension from the paranasal sinuses.

questions.title: In tuberculous meningitis, the subarachnoid exudate is most prominently located where?
questions.question: In tuberculous meningitis, the subarachnoid space is often filled with a gelatinous or fibrinous exudate. Where is this exudate most prominently located?

options.B: At the base of the brain

explanations.A: Incorrect. Exudate over the cerebral convexities, sparing the base, is more characteristic of acute pyogenic bacterial meningitis than tuberculous meningitis.
explanations.B: Correct. Tuberculous meningitis characteristically produces a thick exudate concentrated at the base of the brain, encasing the basal cisterns, circle of Willis and cranial nerves and predisposing to basal vasculitis and hydrocephalus. This basal predilection explains why cranial nerve palsies, obliterative vasculitis and communicating hydrocephalus are classic complications of tuberculous meningitis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The exudate of tuberculous meningitis is a subarachnoid, basal process, not primarily an intraventricular one, although secondary hydrocephalus can follow.
explanations.D: Incorrect. While tuberculous meningitis can extend along the spinal meninges, its most prominent and characteristic location is the base of the brain, not the spinal cord.

questions.learning_objective: State that the subarachnoid exudate of tuberculous meningitis is most prominent at the base of the brain.

questions.title: Which is a well-circumscribed, firm, avascular, spherical intraparenchymal mass associated with TB infection?
questions.question: Which of the following is a well-circumscribed, firm, avascular, spherical intraparenchymal mass associated with Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A gumma is a granulomatous mass lesion of tertiary syphilis (Treponema pallidum), not Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
explanations.B: Correct. Tuberculoma is the well-circumscribed, firm, avascular, spherical intraparenchymal mass formed by coalescing caseating granulomas in CNS tuberculosis, which can mimic a tumour on imaging. On imaging a tuberculoma can be mistaken for a primary or metastatic brain tumour, so tissue diagnosis or a strong epidemiological/clinical context for tuberculosis is often needed.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Cryptococcoma is a mass lesion caused by the fungus Cryptococcus neoformans, typically in immunocompromised patients, not by M. tuberculosis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A cysticercosis cyst is caused by the larval form of the pork tapeworm Taenia solium, a parasitic rather than mycobacterial infection.

questions.learning_objective: Identify tuberculoma as the well-circumscribed, avascular, spherical intraparenchymal mass associated with M. tuberculosis infection.

questions.title: Progressive dementia in advanced HIV is most directly a result of which process?
questions.question: A patient with advanced HIV presents with a progressive dementia. This is most likely a direct result of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. PML, caused by JC virus reactivation, produces focal demyelinating lesions with characteristic imaging findings, not the diffuse progressive dementia of direct HIV CNS infection.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Primary CNS lymphoma presents as a focal mass lesion, not the diffuse cognitive decline that defines HIV-associated dementia.
explanations.C: Correct. HIV-associated dementia results directly from chronic HIV-1 infection of the brain itself (HIV-1 meningoencephalitis), distinct from opportunistic co-infections or other mass-forming complications. This is distinguished from focal HIV-associated CNS lesions such as toxoplasmosis or primary CNS lymphoma, which present with mass effect rather than diffuse cognitive decline.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Toxoplasmosis is an opportunistic protozoal co-infection producing focal necrotising lesions, not the direct viral encephalopathy underlying HIV-associated dementia.

questions.learning_objective: State that progressive dementia in advanced HIV results directly from HIV-1 meningoencephalitis rather than an opportunistic co-infection.

questions.title: Clear CSF, normal opening pressure, 150 WBC/µL lymphocytes, normal glucose, mildly elevated protein — most consistent with?
questions.question: A lumbar puncture is performed on a patient with suspected meningitis. The CSF is clear, with a normal opening pressure, 150 WBC/µL (lymphocytes), normal glucose, and mildly elevated protein. This profile is most consistent with:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Acute bacterial meningitis produces a neutrophil-predominant, markedly low-glucose, turbid CSF, not a clear, lymphocytic, normal-glucose profile.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Tubercular meningitis typically shows a markedly decreased glucose and much higher protein than described here, often with cobweb clot formation.
explanations.C: Correct. A clear CSF with lymphocytic pleocytosis, normal glucose and only mildly elevated protein is the classic profile of viral (aseptic) meningitis. This benign pattern generally allows supportive management without empirical antibiotics once bacterial and tuberculous causes have been reasonably excluded.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Fungal meningitis (e.g. cryptococcal) usually shows a more markedly decreased glucose and higher protein, often in an immunocompromised host, rather than this mild, normal-glucose pattern.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise the clear, normal-glucose, lymphocyte-predominant CSF profile as most consistent with viral (aseptic) meningitis.

questions.title: A brain abscess spreading from a distant infected site is classified as which route of infection?
questions.question: A patient presents with a brain abscess. The causative organism is suspected to have spread from a distant site of infection. This mode of infection is classified as:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Direct implantation describes organisms introduced by trauma or surgery, not bloodstream spread from a distant infected site.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Local extension describes spread from a contiguous adjacent structure (e.g. sinus, ear, tooth), not from a distant site via the bloodstream.
explanations.C: Correct. Spread from a distant infected focus into the brain via the bloodstream is haematogenous seeding, the route by which conditions such as endocarditis or lung abscess cause brain abscess. Haematogenous abscesses are typically found at the grey-white matter junction, where the narrowing vessel calibre favours embolic lodging, and are often multiple.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Peripheral nerve spread describes retrograde axonal transport, as with rabies, not bloodstream dissemination from a distant site.

questions.learning_objective: Classify a brain abscess that spread from a distant infected site as haematogenous.

questions.title: Chronic meningitis, immunocompromised, mixed lymph/monocytic CSF, decreased glucose and chloride — diagnosis?
questions.question: A 60-year-old immunocompromised patient presents with chronic meningitis. CSF analysis shows 200 WBC/µL (mixed lymphocytes and monocytes), decreased glucose, and decreased chloride. This profile is most consistent with:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Viral meningitis typically shows normal glucose and a purely lymphocytic pleocytosis, not the decreased glucose and decreased chloride described here.
explanations.B: Correct. A mixed lymphocytic/monocytic pleocytosis with decreased glucose and decreased chloride, in a chronic meningitic presentation, is the classic CSF picture of tubercular meningitis. Confirmatory testing (CSF acid-fast stain, culture or PCR for M. tuberculosis) is required since the CSF pattern alone is supportive rather than definitive.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Acute pyogenic meningitis produces a neutrophil-predominant pleocytosis with an acute, not chronic, clinical course.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This CSF profile shows clear abnormalities (elevated cell count, decreased glucose and chloride) and is not normal.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise the combination of mixed pleocytosis, decreased glucose and decreased chloride as most consistent with tubercular meningitis.

questions.title: Which complication of a brain abscess can cause rapid, fatal deterioration?
questions.question: A patient presents with a brain abscess. Which of the following is a potential complication of a brain abscess that can lead to a rapid and fatal deterioration?

options.A: Increased intracranial pressure with progressive herniation

explanations.A: Correct. As a brain abscess enlarges it raises intracranial pressure, and unchecked this progresses to brain herniation, compressing the brainstem and causing rapid, often fatal, deterioration. This is why urgent neuroimaging, neurosurgical drainage and control of raised intracranial pressure are central to preventing a fatal outcome.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Reactive gliosis is a reparative astrocytic response at the abscess margin, a chronic-stage finding, not an acutely fatal complication.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Capsule formation marks the chronic, more contained stage of a brain abscess and is a favourable rather than catastrophic development.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Isolated focal neurological deficits, without mass effect or herniation, do not by themselves cause rapid fatal deterioration.

questions.learning_objective: Identify raised intracranial pressure with progressive herniation as the brain abscess complication that can cause rapid fatal deterioration.

questions.title: Encephalitis with temporal/orbital involvement and Cowdry type A intranuclear inclusions — which virus?
questions.question: A young adult presents with encephalitis. MRI shows involvement of the inferior and medial regions of the temporal lobes and orbital gyri. Histology reveals Cowdry type A intranuclear viral inclusion bodies. Which virus is most likely responsible?

explanations.A: Incorrect. JC virus causes progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, a demyelinating white-matter disease in immunocompromised patients, not temporal-lobe encephalitis with Cowdry A bodies.
explanations.B: Correct. Inferior/medial temporal and orbital gyral involvement with Cowdry type A intranuclear inclusion bodies is the classic pattern of HSV-1 encephalitis. Untreated HSV-1 encephalitis has a very high mortality, so empirical intravenous aciclovir is started as soon as the diagnosis is suspected, without waiting for confirmatory PCR.
explanations.C: Incorrect. CMV encephalitis in immunocompromised hosts more typically produces periventricular disease with owl's-eye inclusions, not this temporal-orbital pattern with Cowdry A bodies.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Rabies produces Negri bodies (cytoplasmic, not intranuclear) and characteristically involves the brainstem, hippocampus and cerebellum via peripheral nerve spread.

questions.learning_objective: Identify HSV-1 as the cause of encephalitis with temporal/orbital involvement and Cowdry type A intranuclear inclusion bodies.

questions.title: Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome, complicating acute pyogenic meningitis, is characterised by what?
questions.question: The Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome, a complication of acute pyogenic meningitis, is characterized by:

options.B: Bilateral hemorrhage in the adrenal glands leading to acute adrenal insufficiency
options.D: Rupture of the abscess into the ventricles

explanations.A: Incorrect. Subdural empyema and venous occlusion are separate suppurative complications of CNS infection, not Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome.
explanations.B: Correct. Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome is bilateral haemorrhagic destruction of the adrenal glands, causing acute adrenal insufficiency, DIC and circulatory collapse as a fulminant complication of pyogenic (classically meningococcal) meningitis. It reflects overwhelming meningococcal (or other pyogenic) bacteraemia with septic vasculitis and requires urgent stress-dose corticosteroid replacement alongside antibiotics.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Hydrocephalus from arachnoid fibrosis is a chronic complication of tuberculous meningitis, unrelated to adrenal haemorrhage.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Rupture of an abscess into the ventricles is a catastrophic complication of brain abscess, not of meningococcal septicaemia causing adrenal haemorrhage.

questions.learning_objective: Define Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome as bilateral adrenal haemorrhage causing acute adrenal insufficiency, complicating acute pyogenic meningitis.

questions.title: Which statement regarding viral meningitis is correct?
questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding viral meningitis is correct?

options.A: It is a more fulminant clinical course than pyogenic meningitis.
options.B: The CSF typically shows a marked decrease in glucose.
options.C: The clinical course is usually self-limiting and treated symptomatically.
options.D: The most common causative virus is Herpes Simplex Virus.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Viral meningitis runs a milder, not more fulminant, course than acute pyogenic bacterial meningitis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. CSF glucose is characteristically preserved (normal), not markedly decreased, in viral meningitis.
explanations.C: Correct. Viral meningitis is typically a benign, self-limiting illness managed with supportive, symptomatic care rather than specific antiviral treatment. Antibiotics are withheld once bacterial and other treatable causes have been reasonably excluded, since they offer no benefit against the causative virus.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Enterovirus, not Herpes Simplex Virus, is the most common cause of viral (aseptic) meningitis.

questions.learning_objective: State that viral meningitis usually runs a self-limiting clinical course, treated symptomatically.

questions.title: Perivascular/parenchymal mononuclear infiltrates, microglial nodules and neuronophagia are most characteristic of what?
questions.question: A pathologist notes perivascular and parenchymal mononuclear cell infiltrates, microglial nodules, and neuronophagia in a brain tissue sample. This microscopic picture is most characteristic of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Brain abscess shows a central zone of liquefactive necrosis surrounded by a fibrous/granulation-tissue capsule, a different pattern from diffuse mononuclear infiltration.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Pyogenic meningitis is characterised by a neutrophilic exudate over the meninges, not mononuclear parenchymal infiltrates with neuronophagia.
explanations.C: Correct. Perivascular and parenchymal mononuclear infiltrates with microglial nodules and neuronophagia is the classic histological picture of viral encephalitis. This pattern reflects both direct viral infection of neurons and the cell-mediated immune response clearing infected cells.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Tuberculoma shows caseating granulomatous inflammation with epithelioid histiocytes and Langhans giant cells, not the mononuclear/microglial-nodule pattern of viral encephalitis.

questions.learning_objective: Identify perivascular/parenchymal mononuclear infiltrates, microglial nodules and neuronophagia as characteristic of viral encephalitis.

questions.title: A subdural empyema complicating acute meningitis is most directly related to spread from which source?
questions.question: A patient presents with acute meningitis and is found to have a subdural empyema. This complication is most directly related to the spread of infection from which of the following?

options.A: Hematogenous seeding from a distant site
options.B: Direct implantation during a surgical procedure
options.C: Infection of the skull or air sinuses

explanations.A: Incorrect. Haematogenous seeding from a distant site is a less common route for subdural empyema than direct contiguous spread from the sinuses or skull.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Iatrogenic direct implantation is a recognised but less common cause than local extension from paranasal sinus or skull infection.
explanations.C: Correct. Subdural empyema most directly results from local extension of infection from the paranasal sinuses, middle ear/mastoid, or an infected skull. Because the subdural space offers little anatomical barrier, subdural empyema from these sources can spread and deteriorate rapidly, making it a neurosurgical emergency.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Travel through peripheral nerves is the rabies virus route, unrelated to the contiguous spread that produces subdural empyema.

questions.learning_objective: State that subdural empyema most directly relates to spread of infection from the skull or paranasal sinuses.

questions.title: CSF findings expected in a patient with a brain abscess undergoing lumbar puncture?
questions.question: A patient with a brain abscess undergoes a lumbar puncture. Which of the following CSF findings would be expected?

options.A: Markedly decreased glucose with very high protein
options.B: Normal glucose with elevated WBC and elevated protein
options.C: Normal glucose with a lymphocytic predominance and normal protein
options.D: Markedly elevated neutrophils with very low protein

explanations.A: Incorrect. Markedly decreased glucose with very high protein describes bacterial or tuberculous meningitis, where the CSF space itself is directly infected, not the parameningeal reaction of a walled-off abscess.
explanations.B: Correct. Brain abscess typically produces a parameningeal reaction with normal CSF glucose but elevated WBC and protein, since the infection is contained within brain parenchyma rather than the CSF space. Lumbar puncture in a patient with a suspected brain abscess is nonetheless generally avoided because of the risk of precipitating herniation from the mass effect.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Normal protein would be an under-reaction; a parameningeal inflammatory response from an adjacent abscess typically elevates CSF protein.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Markedly elevated neutrophils with very low protein does not fit either the abscess pattern (normal glucose, moderate elevation) or any classic meningitis pattern.

questions.learning_objective: State that CSF in brain abscess typically shows normal glucose with elevated WBC and protein, unlike meningitis.

questions.title: A spinal block from arachnoid fibrosis in TB meningitis most likely causes which CSF protein change?
questions.question: In tuberculous meningitis, the presence of a spinal block due to arachnoid fibrosis would most likely cause which of the following changes in the CSF protein level?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A normal protein level would not be expected once a mechanical spinal block obstructs normal CSF circulation and clearance.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Protein rises rather than decreases below a spinal block, due to stasis and increased local vascular permeability.
explanations.C: Correct. A spinal subarachnoid block from arachnoid fibrosis obstructs normal CSF flow and protein clearance, causing markedly elevated CSF protein below the block, sometimes several hundred mg/dL. This markedly elevated protein below the block can occasionally produce CSF xanthochromia and very high viscosity (Froin syndrome) when the block is complete.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A mechanical block produces a marked, not absent, change in CSF protein.

questions.learning_objective: State that a spinal block from arachnoid fibrosis in tuberculous meningitis causes markedly elevated CSF protein.

questions.title: Which statement is true regarding the gross appearance of acute pyogenic meningitis?
questions.question: Which of the following statements is true regarding the gross appearance of acute pyogenic meningitis?

options.A: The subarachnoid space is clear and normal
options.B: The pia-arachnoid is thickened and fibrotic
options.C: The CSF is turbid and the leptomeninges are congested
options.D: Discrete white granules are scattered on the leptomeninges

explanations.A: Incorrect. A clear, normal subarachnoid space is inconsistent with active pyogenic meningitis, which produces a purulent exudate.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Thickened, fibrotic pia-arachnoid describes a chronic process such as healed tuberculous meningitis, not the acute pyogenic picture.
explanations.C: Correct. Acute pyogenic meningitis grossly shows turbid, purulent CSF with congested, hyperaemic leptomeninges, most marked over the convexities. The purulent exudate can also extend along the subarachnoid space to coat the cranial nerve roots, producing cranial neuropathies in severe cases.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Discrete white granules scattered on the leptomeninges is more suggestive of meningeal carcinomatosis or miliary tuberculosis than acute pyogenic meningitis.

questions.learning_objective: State that the gross appearance of acute pyogenic meningitis is turbid CSF with congested leptomeninges.

questions.title: The route of entry for rabies virus into the nervous system is primarily which?
questions.question: The route of entry for the rabies virus into the nervous system is primarily:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Rabies virus does not primarily disseminate via the bloodstream to reach the CNS.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Direct implantation describes trauma or surgical introduction of organisms, not the neurotropic transport rabies virus uses.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Local extension describes contiguous spread from an adjacent infected structure, not the retrograde axonal route rabies uses from a distant bite site.
explanations.D: Correct. Rabies virus travels retrograde along peripheral nerve axons from the site of inoculation (typically an animal bite) to the spinal cord and brain, a route unique among the classic causes of CNS infection. The incubation period therefore varies with the distance from the bite site to the CNS, and once symptomatic, rabies is almost universally fatal.

questions.learning_objective: State that rabies virus reaches the CNS primarily by retrograde travel through peripheral nerves.

questions.title: Which intracytoplasmic inclusion body is found in neurons of a patient with rabies?
questions.question: What is the characteristic intracytoplasmic inclusion body found in neurons of a patient with rabies?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Cowdry type A bodies are intranuclear (not intracytoplasmic) inclusions characteristic of HSV and CMV infection.
explanations.B: Correct. Negri bodies are eosinophilic, round-to-oval intracytoplasmic inclusions in rabies-infected neurons, classically seen in cerebellar Purkinje cells and hippocampal pyramidal neurons, and are diagnostic of rabies. Their identification confirms the diagnosis, historically by light microscopy and now more often by direct fluorescent antibody testing of brain tissue.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Lewy bodies are intracytoplasmic alpha-synuclein aggregates seen in Parkinson disease and dementia with Lewy bodies, unrelated to viral infection.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Bunina bodies are small eosinophilic inclusions seen in motor neurons in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, not rabies.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the Negri body as the characteristic intracytoplasmic inclusion body of rabies-infected neurons.

questions.title: Subacute meningitis, cobweb-forming CSF, 300 WBC/µL mixed lymphocytic predominance — most likely etiology?
questions.question: A patient presents with subacute meningitis. The CSF is slightly opaque with a cobweb formation. The cell count is 300 WBC/µL with a mixed lymphocytic predominance. Which of the following is the most likely etiology?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Viral meningitis produces a clear (not opaque or cobweb-forming) CSF with a purely lymphocytic, not mixed, pleocytosis.
explanations.B: Correct. A subacute course with slightly opaque, cobweb-forming CSF and a mixed lymphocytic pleocytosis is the classic pattern of tuberculous meningitis, the cobweb clot reflecting the high protein content. Acid-fast staining, mycobacterial culture or PCR of this CSF is used to confirm the diagnosis, since culture can take several weeks.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Pyogenic bacterial meningitis is acute, not subacute, and produces a neutrophil-predominant, turbid (not cobweb-forming) CSF.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Fungal meningitis is a differential for subacute/chronic meningitis but does not classically produce the described cobweb clot, which is specific to the high-protein tuberculous pattern.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise subacute meningitis with cobweb CSF and mixed lymphocytic pleocytosis as most likely tubercular.

questions.title: Which of the following is NOT a route of entry for organisms into the nervous system?
questions.question: All of the following are routes of entry for organisms into the nervous system EXCEPT:

options.D: Trans-synaptic diffusion through the blood-brain barrier

explanations.A: Incorrect as the exception — haematogenous spread is one of the four recognised routes of CNS infectious entry.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the exception — direct implantation (trauma or iatrogenic) is one of the four recognised routes.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the exception — retrograde axonal transport along peripheral nerves (as with rabies) is a recognised route.
explanations.D: Correct. "Trans-synaptic diffusion through the blood-brain barrier" is not a recognised route of CNS infectious entry — the barrier is a vascular/glial interface, and peripheral-nerve spread occurs by retrograde axonal transport, not synaptic diffusion across it. Recognising the four true routes precisely matters clinically, since it directs the search for the underlying source of a given CNS infection.

questions.learning_objective: Identify trans-synaptic diffusion through the blood-brain barrier as not a recognised route of CNS infectious entry.

questions.title: A brain abscess following a penetrating head injury represents which route of entry?
questions.question: A patient develops a brain abscess following a penetrating head injury. This represents which route of entry?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Haematogenous spread is bloodstream seeding from a distant site, not organisms introduced through a traumatic skull breach.
explanations.B: Correct. A penetrating head injury physically breaches the skull and dura, directly implanting organisms (typically skin or soil flora) into the brain — direct implantation. Traumatic implantation typically carries skin or soil flora directly into the wound tract, so surgical debridement and antibiotic prophylaxis are standard after such injuries.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Local extension describes contiguous spread from an adjacent infected structure such as a sinus or ear, not a traumatic wound tract.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Peripheral nerve spread is the rabies-type route, unrelated to traumatic implantation.

questions.learning_objective: Classify a brain abscess following a penetrating head injury as spread by direct implantation.

field_notes.asu: MCQs - cerebellar tumlors & CNS infection.pdf, item 37

questions.title: In viral meningitis, the CSF glucose level is most often what?
questions.question: In viral meningitis, the CSF glucose level is most often:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Markedly decreased glucose is the pattern of acute bacterial meningitis, not viral meningitis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A moderate decrease is more typical of tuberculous or fungal meningitis, not viral meningitis.
explanations.C: Correct. CSF glucose in viral (aseptic) meningitis is most often nearly always normal, reflecting the absence of bacterial/neutrophil glucose consumption. This preserved glucose, together with a lymphocytic pleocytosis and clear CSF, is the key laboratory clue used to favour a benign viral cause over bacterial or tuberculous meningitis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. CSF glucose does not become elevated in meningitis of any cause; it tracks serum glucose at most and is typically normal or reduced, never significantly elevated as a disease feature.

questions.learning_objective: State that CSF glucose in viral meningitis is most often nearly always normal.

field_notes.asu: MCQs - cerebellar tumlors & CNS infection.pdf, item 39

questions.title: What does the presence of microglial nodules indicate in acute encephalitis?
questions.question: A patient presents with acute encephalitis. The microscopic examination of brain tissue shows perivascular cuffing with mononuclear cells and microglial nodules. What does the presence of microglial nodules indicate?

options.C: A reaction to viral infection or neuronal injury

explanations.A: Incorrect. Acute bacterial infection produces a neutrophilic response, not microglial nodules, which are a mononuclear/microglial reactive pattern typical of viral infection.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Microglial nodules reflect a reaction to neuronal injury/infection, not a demyelinating process, which would instead show myelin loss with relative axon preservation.
explanations.C: Correct. Microglial nodules represent activated microglia clustering around damaged or virally infected neurons, indicating a reactive response to viral infection or neuronal injury. Their presence indicates active tissue injury and an ongoing inflammatory/immune reaction rather than pointing to a specific virus or a distinct disease mechanism such as demyelination.
explanations.D: Incorrect. While microglial activation can occur in prion disease, the specific combination here (perivascular cuffing plus microglial nodules) is the classic viral encephalitis pattern, not the spongiform change characteristic of prion disease.

questions.learning_objective: State that microglial nodules indicate a reaction to viral infection or neuronal injury.

field_notes.asu: MCQs - cerebellar tumlors & CNS infection.pdf, item 40

questions.title: A moderate decrease in CSF glucose in TB meningitis is most useful in differentiating it from which condition?
questions.question: A patient with tuberculous meningitis has a CSF sample that shows a moderate decrease in glucose. This finding is most useful in differentiating tuberculous meningitis from:

explanations.A: Correct. Viral meningitis characteristically preserves a normal CSF glucose, so a moderate decrease helps distinguish tuberculous meningitis from a viral cause. This intermediate glucose level, together with a mixed lymphocytic/monocytic pleocytosis and elevated protein, helps triage an ambiguous chronic meningitis picture toward tuberculosis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Fungal meningitis can also show a moderately-to-markedly decreased glucose, overlapping with tuberculous meningitis rather than being clearly distinguished by this finding.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Pyogenic meningitis shows a markedly, not moderately, decreased glucose, so the two are already distinguishable by degree rather than needing this comparison.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Comparing to normal CSF is not a clinically meaningful differential in this context; the relevant comparison is against other infectious meningitides.

questions.learning_objective: State that a moderate CSF glucose decrease helps differentiate tuberculous meningitis from viral meningitis.

field_notes.asu: MCQs - cerebellar tumlors & CNS infection.pdf, item 42

questions.title: A CNS infection acquired as a complication of a surgical procedure is best described as which route?
questions.question: A patient presents with a CNS infection that was acquired as a complication of a surgical procedure. This route of infection is best described as:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Haematogenous spread describes bloodstream seeding from a distant infected focus, not a breach created by the surgical procedure itself.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Local extension describes contiguous spread from an adjacent infected structure, not a barrier breach created by a medical procedure.
explanations.C: Correct. A CNS infection acquired as a complication of a surgical procedure is iatrogenic direct implantation, a subtype of direct implantation where the barrier breach is created by the intervention itself. Recognising this route is important for infection control, since it points to procedural asepsis rather than a distant or contiguous source as the point of entry.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Peripheral nerve spread is the rabies-type route, unrelated to a surgical breach of the CNS barriers.

questions.learning_objective: Classify a CNS infection acquired as a complication of a surgical procedure as iatrogenic direct implantation.

field_notes.asu: MCQs - cerebellar tumlors & CNS infection.pdf, item 44

questions.title: Chronic meningitis, immunocompetent, no fungal exposure, moderate mononuclear increase, elevated protein, moderate glucose decrease — most likely diagnosis?
questions.question: A patient presents with chronic meningitis. The CSF shows a moderate increase in mononuclear cells, elevated protein, and moderately decreased glucose. The patient is immunocompetent and has no known exposure to fungi. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Viral meningitis is typically acute and self-limiting with normal glucose, not a chronic course with decreased glucose.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Fungal meningitis is less likely given the explicit absence of any fungal exposure history.
explanations.C: Correct. Chronic meningitis with a moderate mononuclear pleocytosis, elevated protein and moderately decreased glucose, in an immunocompetent host with no fungal exposure, is most consistent with tuberculous meningitis. Confirmatory testing (CSF acid-fast stain, culture or nucleic acid amplification for tuberculosis) is still required, since the CSF pattern alone is supportive rather than definitive.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Meningeal carcinomatosis requires an underlying malignancy, not suggested here, and is not the most likely diagnosis in an otherwise unremarkable immunocompetent patient.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise chronic meningitis with moderate mononuclear pleocytosis, elevated protein and moderately decreased glucose, in an immunocompetent host with no fungal exposure, as most likely tuberculous.

questions.title: A brain abscess caused by systemic pyaemia is likely to show which finding on neuroimaging?
questions.question: A patient with a brain abscess caused by systemic pyaemia is likely to have which of the following findings on neuroimaging?

options.A: A single large abscess in the frontal lobe
options.B: Multiple small abscesses throughout the brain

explanations.A: Incorrect. A single large abscess is more typical of a contiguous local-extension source (e.g. sinusitis) than of disseminated systemic pyaemia.
explanations.B: Correct. Systemic pyaemia seeds the brain haematogenously at multiple sites simultaneously, typically producing multiple small abscesses scattered through the brain, often at the grey-white junction. This multi-focal, haematogenous pattern should prompt a search for the primary source, such as infective endocarditis or another disseminated septic focus.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Subdural empyema is a distinct suppurative collection in the subdural space, not the intraparenchymal multi-abscess pattern of haematogenous seeding.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Epidural abscess is a separate entity, typically related to skull osteomyelitis or spinal infection, not the haematogenous multi-focal brain abscess pattern.

questions.learning_objective: State that a brain abscess from systemic pyaemia typically shows multiple small abscesses on neuroimaging.

field_notes.asu: MCQs - cerebellar tumlors & CNS infection.pdf, item 46

questions.title: The most common route of entry for organisms causing a brain abscess is which?
questions.question: The most common route of entry for organisms causing a brain abscess is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Direct implantation is a recognised but less common overall route than haematogenous spread.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Local extension is an important route for specific sources (sinuses, ear) but is not the single most common route across all brain abscess causes.
explanations.C: Correct. Haematogenous spread from a distant infected focus is the most common overall route of entry for organisms causing brain abscess. This is particularly true for brain abscesses that are multiple or located at the grey-white matter junction, a classic haematogenous distribution.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Travel through peripheral nerves is specific to a small number of neurotropic pathogens such as rabies virus, not a common route for typical pyogenic brain abscess.

questions.learning_objective: State that haematogenous spread is the most common overall route of entry for brain abscess.

field_notes.asu: MCQs - cerebellar tumlors & CNS infection.pdf, item 47

questions.title: A subdural empyema is located in the space between which two structures?
questions.question: A patient presents with a subdural empyema. This infection is located in the space between the:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The space between skull and dura mater is the epidural space, the location of an epidural abscess, not subdural empyema.
explanations.B: Correct. Subdural empyema occupies the subdural space, the potential space between the dura mater and the arachnoid mater, which offers little barrier to rapid spread. Because this space offers little anatomical resistance, infection introduced here can spread rapidly across a hemisphere, making prompt drainage important.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The space between arachnoid and pia mater is the subarachnoid space, containing CSF and the site of meningitis, not subdural empyema.
explanations.D: Incorrect. There is no potential space between pia mater and brain parenchyma in the relevant sense here; this option does not correspond to a named CNS infection compartment.

questions.learning_objective: State that subdural empyema occupies the space between the dura mater and the arachnoid mater.

field_notes.asu: MCQs - cerebellar tumlors & CNS infection.pdf, item 48

questions.title: A temporoparietal brain abscess via local extension most likely arises from which source?
questions.question: A patient presents with a brain abscess. The abscess is located in the temporoparietal region. What is the most likely source of infection if the spread was via local extension?

explanations.A: Correct. The temporal lobe lies directly adjacent to the middle ear and mastoid, so otitis media (or mastoiditis) is the most likely source of a temporoparietal brain abscess spreading by local extension. This is distinguished from frontal lobe abscesses, which more often arise by local extension from frontal sinusitis rather than ear disease.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Frontal sinusitis characteristically causes abscesses in the frontal lobe, adjacent to the frontal sinus, not the temporoparietal region.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A dental infection more typically tracks to structures near the jaw and lower face, not specifically the temporoparietal region.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Penetrating trauma is a direct implantation route, not local extension, and this question specifies spread was via local extension.

questions.learning_objective: State that a temporoparietal brain abscess by local extension most often arises from otitis media.

field_notes.asu: MCQs - cerebellar tumlors & CNS infection.pdf, item 49

questions.title: Which virus is most commonly associated with viral (aseptic) meningitis?
questions.question: Which of the following viruses is most commonly associated with viral (aseptic) meningitis?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV-1) more typically causes focal encephalitis, and while HSV-2 can cause recurrent aseptic meningitis, it is not the most common overall cause.
explanations.B: Incorrect. JC virus causes progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy in immunocompromised patients, not viral meningitis.
explanations.C: Correct. Enteroviruses (coxsackieviruses, echoviruses) are collectively the most common cause of viral (aseptic) meningitis worldwide, typically producing a mild, self-limiting, often seasonal illness. It typically produces a mild, self-limiting illness, especially in children, and often occurs in seasonal outbreaks, particularly in the summer and early autumn.
explanations.D: Incorrect. HIV can rarely cause an aseptic meningitis during acute seroconversion, but it is not the most common overall cause of viral meningitis.

questions.learning_objective: State that enterovirus is the virus most commonly associated with viral (aseptic) meningitis.

field_notes.asu: MCQs - cerebellar tumlors & CNS infection.pdf, item 51

questions.title: Progressive focal deficits in a patient with a brain abscess are a direct result of what?
questions.question: A patient with a brain abscess is at risk of progressive focal deficits. These deficits are a direct result of:

options.B: The mass effect and destruction of brain tissue by the abscess

explanations.A: Incorrect. Systemic infection and fever are constitutional features of the illness, not the direct mechanism producing a focal neurological deficit.
explanations.B: Correct. Progressive focal deficits from a brain abscess result directly from the combination of local tissue destruction and mass effect compressing adjacent functioning brain. Recognising this distinction matters clinically, since meningeal irritation and hydrocephalus are managed differently from a focal, mass-effect-driven parenchymal lesion.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Meningeal irritation produces neck stiffness and headache, a meningismus syndrome, not focal deficits from a parenchymal lesion.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Hydrocephalus, when present, produces a more generalised syndrome of raised intracranial pressure rather than the localised, mass-effect-driven focal deficits described here.

questions.learning_objective: State that progressive focal deficits from a brain abscess result directly from mass effect and destruction of brain tissue.

field_notes.asu: MCQs - cerebellar tumlors & CNS infection.pdf, item 53

questions.title: A CNS infection secondary to osteomyelitis of the skull represents which route of entry?
questions.question: A patient develops a CNS infection secondary to osteomyelitis of the skull. This represents which route of entry?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Haematogenous spread describes bloodstream seeding from a distant site, not direct spread from adjacent infected bone.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Direct implantation refers to organisms introduced by trauma or a procedure, not contiguous spread from infected bone.
explanations.C: Correct. Infected skull bone lies in direct contiguity with the intracranial contents, so osteomyelitis of the skull spreading to the CNS is local extension. This route is distinct from a haematogenous or traumatic-implantation abscess and should prompt treatment of the underlying bone infection alongside the intracranial one.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Peripheral nerve spread is the rabies-type route, unrelated to contiguous bone infection.

questions.learning_objective: Classify a CNS infection secondary to skull osteomyelitis as spread by local extension.

field_notes.asu: MCQs - cerebellar tumlors & CNS infection.pdf, item 56

questions.title: A brain abscess with a well-developed capsule indicates which stage?
questions.question: A patient presents with a brain abscess that has formed a well-developed capsule. This indicates the abscess is in which stage?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The acute stage of brain abscess is diffuse cerebritis, without a well-developed capsule.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A well-developed, mature capsule reflects the later, chronic stage rather than an intermediate subacute stage of early capsule formation.
explanations.C: Correct. A well-developed fibrous capsule walling off the necrotic centre marks the chronic (late capsule) stage of brain abscess evolution. This later, more contained stage is generally more amenable to surgical drainage than the earlier, diffuse cerebritis stage, when the lesion is poorly demarcated.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Resolving" is not a standard staging term for brain abscess evolution, which is described as cerebritis (early/late) progressing to capsule formation (early/late).

questions.learning_objective: State that a well-developed capsule in a brain abscess indicates the chronic stage.

field_notes.asu: MCQs - cerebellar tumlors & CNS infection.pdf, item 57

questions.title: Which is a characteristic shared by both tuberculous and fungal meningitis?
questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic of both tuberculous and fungal meningitis?

options.B: The CSF shows a lymphocytic predominance and decreased glucose
options.C: The infection is always acute and fulminant
options.D: The causative organisms are always bacteria

explanations.A: Incorrect. CSF glucose is characteristically decreased, not normal, in both tuberculous and fungal meningitis.
explanations.B: Correct. Both tuberculous and fungal meningitis characteristically produce a lymphocyte-predominant pleocytosis with decreased CSF glucose and elevated protein, a shared chronic-meningitis pattern distinguished by specific stains and cultures. The two are ultimately distinguished from each other by specific stains, cultures and antigen tests (such as India ink or cryptococcal antigen) rather than by this shared CSF profile alone.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Both are typically chronic or subacute in course, not acute and fulminant, which better describes pyogenic bacterial meningitis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Fungal meningitis is, by definition, caused by fungi, not bacteria, so the causative organisms are not always bacteria.

questions.learning_objective: State that tuberculous and fungal meningitis share a lymphocytic, decreased-glucose CSF pattern, distinguishing both from viral and pyogenic causes.
